items.prose: A quant scans 30 independent signals on noise, each tested at $\alpha = 0.05$.
items.question: What is the chance at least one looks significant? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 1 minus the chance that all 30 stay quiet.

byKey.added: You added 30 chances of 0.05 and got more than 1. A chance cannot exceed 1: use the complement.
byKey.none: That is the chance all 30 stay quiet.

explain.text: All 30 quiet has chance $0.95^{30} = 0.215$. So at least one false alarm has chance 0.785. Nearly four scans in five find a noise signal that passes.

items.prose: Six signals give sorted $p$-values 0.001, 0.009, 0.020, 0.030, 0.12 and 0.40. Use BH with $\alpha = 0.05$.
items.question: How many signals does BH reject?

feedback.correct: Four: ranks 1 to 4 sit under their bars.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $p_{(k)}$ with $k \times 0.05 / 6$ and keep up to the largest rank that passes.

byKey.bonf: That is Bonferroni, $p \le 0.0083$. BH gives later ranks higher bars.
byKey.five: Rank 5 has $p = 0.12$, far above its bar of 0.0417.

explain.text: The bars are 0.0083, 0.0167, 0.025, 0.0333, 0.0417 and 0.05. Ranks 1 to 4 sit under theirs, rank 5 does not. BH rejects 4; Bonferroni would reject only the first.

items.prose: A strategy has an annualised Sharpe ratio of 0.7 over 16 years.
items.question: What is its $t$ statistic?

byKey.divide: You divided by $\sqrt T$. Multiply by it.

explain.text: The standard error is $1/\sqrt{16} = 0.25$, so $t = 0.7 / 0.25 = 2.8$. As one strategy fixed in advance, that is strong evidence: one-sided $p = 0.003$.

items.prose: A backtest ranks stocks on annual earnings from the day each financial year ends. In reality the reports come out about two months later.
items.question: Which flaw is this?

options.why: Survivorship drops firms that failed. Here every firm is in; the problem is when the data were known.
Nothing was chosen from many tries. The flaw is using numbers before they were published.

options.text: No flaw: the earnings are real numbers
options.why: They are real, but a trader could not have seen them on that day.

feedback.correct: Using earnings two months before they were public is look-ahead.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask when a trader could first have seen the numbers.

explain.text: The backtest trades on numbers that were published two months later. That is look-ahead bias, a cousin of snooping. The fix is to use each figure from its release date.

items.prose: A screen runs 200 tests at $\alpha = 0.01$. Every null is true.
items.question: How many false discoveries does it expect?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the number of tests by $\alpha$.

byKey.five: That uses 0.05. This screen tests at 0.01.
byKey.one: Each test adds 0.01 to the expected count: 200 of them add 2.

explain.text: Each true null is rejected with chance 0.01, and expectations add. So 200 tests expect $200 \times 0.01 = 2$ false discoveries. The chance of at least one is $1 - 0.99^{200} = 0.87$.

items.prose: Two desks. A fund will trade every signal it accepts, and one false signal is costly. A research team builds a shortlist of stocks to study further, and a few false leads are fine.
items.question: Which control suits each?

options.text: FWER (Bonferroni) for the fund, FDR (BH) for the shortlist
FDR (BH) for the fund, FWER (Bonferroni) for the shortlist
options.why: You swapped them. The fund cannot afford even one false signal, which is the FWER's guarantee.

options.text: BH for both, since it finds more
options.why: BH finds more by allowing a share of false ones. The fund wants to avoid even one.
Without a correction both desks would act on many noise signals.

feedback.correct: One costly error calls for the FWER; a tolerable share calls for the FDR.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match each desk's tolerance for false signals to a method.

explain.text: The fund cares about the chance of any false signal: that is the FWER, held by Bonferroni. The shortlist can live with a small share of false leads: that is the FDR, held by BH. BH will also find more.

items.prose: A manager tried 20 strategies over 4 years and shows the best. The one-sided Bonferroni bar on $t$ is $z_{1 - 0.05/20} = 2.81$.
items.question: What Sharpe ratio must the best clear? Give 2 decimal places.

widget.label: Sharpe the best of 20 must clear

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the bar on $t$ by $\sqrt T$.

byKey.t: That is the bar on $t$. Divide by $\sqrt 4 = 2$ for a Sharpe.
byKey.one: That is the one-test bar, $1.645 / 2$. She tried 20.
byKey.T: You divided by $T = 4$. Divide by $\sqrt T = 2$.

explain.text: A Sharpe of SR over 4 years has $t = 2\,\mathrm{SR}$. Clearing $t = 2.81$ needs $\mathrm{SR} \ge 1.40$. With one strategy the bar would be only 0.82.

items.prose: A team reports a new factor with $t = 2.6$. It was the best of 400 definitions they tried.
items.question: How should you read it?

options.text: Not convincing: it misses the $t > 3$ bar, and 400 tries ask for more

options.why: You used the one-test bar. With 400 tries, about 18 noise factors would clear 2.
That $p$ is for one test. Bonferroni over 400 makes it $400 \times 0.009 = 3.7$, capped at 1.
They can. This one needs a bar fit for 400 tries, above 3.

feedback.correct: The best of 400 at $t = 2.6$ is what noise produces.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many factors could pass by luck at this bar.

explain.text: Among 400 noise factors, about $400 \times 0.0455 = 18$ show $|t| > 2$, and about $400 \times 0.0093 = 3.7$ show $|t| > 2.6$. So 2.6 from the best of 400 is unremarkable. That is why Harvey, Liu and Zhu ask for $t > 3$.
